text_summary.body: That night Belshazzar the Chaldean king was killed, and Darius the Mede received the kingdom, about sixty-two years old.

setting.period: October 539 BC (if "that night" is the night of the capture)
setting.body: The Chronicle records the entry of Ugbaru and Cyrus's army on 16 Tašrītu, Cyrus's own entry on 3 Arahsamna, Gubaru's appointment of officials, and Ugbaru's death on 11 Arahsamna. No Babylonian source records Belshazzar's fate.

constraints.textual_assertion: your kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians … In that night Belshazzar … was slain. Darius the Mede received the kingdom
assumptions: Daniel does not date "that night" or name the capture; this constraint assumes it is the night Babylon was entered (16 Tašrītu). Babylonian sources do not record Belshazzar's death; if he died elsewhere or earlier, this constraint does not hold.

locations.role: Place of the king's death (as narrated)

competing_reconstructions.label: Gubaru/Ugbaru (Cyrus's governor)
competing_reconstructions.summary: Darius was a sub-king installed by Cyrus, known from the Chronicle as Ugbaru (who entered Babylon and died within a month) or Gubaru (who appointed officials). Problems: neither is called a Mede or king, and the Chronicle's two spellings may be two men.

competing_reconstructions.label: Cyrus himself
competing_reconstructions.summary: Reads Dan 6:28 as "the reign of Darius, that is, the reign of Cyrus the Persian". Wiseman's argument is known here only through Wikipedia (his essay is registered at metadata level).

competing_reconstructions.label: Cyaxares II, son of Astyages
competing_reconstructions.summary: Josephus makes Darius the son of Astyages with another Greek name; Xenophon names Astyages' son Cyaxares as Median king and Cyrus's uncle. Cyaxares II is unattested outside Xenophon.

competing_reconstructions.label: Cambyses II
proponents: Named in the literature; no proponent identified in the sources read
competing_reconstructions.summary: Cyrus's son was installed in Babylon; the objection is that he was neither a Mede nor 62.

competing_reconstructions.label: Literary figure modelled on Darius I and the prophecies of the Medes
competing_reconstructions.summary: No such king can be fitted into the known sequence; the author projected Darius I into the past to fulfil prophecies that the Medes would take Babylon (Isa 13:17; Jer 51:11, 28). Described by Wikipedia as the majority view.

commentary.paraphrase: Guzik identifies Darius the Mede with Gubaru, a sub-king ruling Babylon under Cyrus, and notes his age of about sixty-two.

open_questions: Locate the Gubaru texts in later Babylonian contracts (not read).
